text:
Direct evidence supports increasing training negatives and testing sampled softmax, but does not establish eight negatives as optimal for this benchmark. Klenitskiy and Vasilev keep SASRec’s architecture fixed and replace one-negative BCE with full or sampled cross-entropy. On Amazon Beauty, full-catalog HR@10 rises from 0.0246 to 0.0533 with full cross-entropy; 3,000-negative sampled cross-entropy reaches 0.0490. Their negative-count sweep suggests approximately 1,000 negatives as a practical option, depending on dataset. These are different data and evaluation conditions, with early stopping rather than equal GPU-time budgets. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.07602)

Loss calibration is another confound: gSASRec attributes degradation partly to overconfidence induced by negative sampling and introduces generalized BCE. Its experiments support comparing BCE, gBCE and sampled softmax at matched negative counts; they do not establish an eight-negative optimum on these four Amazon categories. Separately, a SASRec study covering Amazon Beauty finds that uniform sampling favors head items, while popularity and in-batch sampling can improve balance at an aggregate accuracy cost. Report head/mid/tail validation diagnostics using training-derived popularity. [gSASRec](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.07192), [sampling study](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.17276v1)

Recommended controls, inferred from these findings: cross loss with negative count, including eight as a candidate; hold architecture, batches and sampler fixed; exclude padding, the current positive and known training-history positives; track duplicate negatives. Unobserved items remain potentially positive, so history exclusion cannot eliminate false negatives. Compare uniform sampling against a modest popularity mixture separately. Measure validation HR@10 against cumulative single-GPU seconds, with identical tuning budgets and pinned evaluation candidates; equal epochs alone do not establish compute fairness.
